title: Ordinary Witness: Speaking of Jesus Without the Script
subtitle: A five-session study on telling the truth about Jesus the way a witness tells the truth, not the way a salesman closes a deal.
summary:
This study is for the ordinary Christian who has quietly decided that evangelism is for other people. For the one who flinches when the word comes up, who has watched the bad versions of it and wanted nothing to do with them, who loves Jesus and would still rather do almost anything than bring his name up at the dinner table. It is also for the seeker and the skeptic in the room, the friend who has been handled before and would like, just once, to be met instead. It walks slowly through what it actually means to speak of Jesus without a script, one movement at a time. Why we dread it, and which fears are wisdom and which are caricature. What a witness is, against the salesman who closes and the arguer who wins. The life lived together that makes the question askable before a word is ever said. The telling of your own story, honest about the doubt and the cost, not packaged into a tidy before-and-after. And the long patience of friendship and God's own timing, evangelism as a table you keep setting rather than a decision you pressure.

This is not a study that will hand anyone a technique. It will refuse that on purpose, because the technique is most of what went wrong. Witness is not a sales process and a person is not a target, and the moment we treat them as one we have already lost the thing we were sent to give. Bell knows the dread from the inside, and he knows the other side of it too. He came to faith from atheism. He was, for years, the man being witnessed to, and most of the people who tried got it wrong, treated him as a project to be closed rather than a person to be known. He is not standing over this study explaining evangelism to the reluctant. He is one of them. He has frozen at the table. He has said nothing when he should have spoken and said too much when he should have listened. He writes from inside the fear, and the leader will lead from there too.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: The Fear and the Caricature
sessions.aim: To bring the dread of evangelism into the light and look at it honestly, separating the fears that are actually wisdom from the caricatures we have absorbed, and to name and refuse the bad models, the salesman, the tract-pusher, the argument-winner, before pretending we are above them.
sessions.summary: Most Christians dread evangelism, and almost no one says so out loud in church, because admitting it feels like admitting you do not love Jesus enough. So we carry the dread privately and let it harden into avoidance. The first question of this whole study is not how to do it but why we cannot bring ourselves to. Bell takes the fear at full strength, because he carries it himself. Some of the dread is shame, the suspicion that a real Christian would not feel this way. But some of it is wisdom. We have all seen evangelism done as a sales pitch, a cornering, an argument to be won, a stranger reduced to a target, and the part of us that recoils from that is not weak faith. It is a true instinct that something is wrong with the picture we were handed. The session names the three bad models plainly. The salesman, who is closing a deal and treats a soul as a conversion to be notched. The tract-pusher, who hands over a leaflet instead of a self and calls it obedience. The argument-winner, who would rather be right than be trusted, who wins the point and loses the person. Then the turn, and it is a hard one. Before we sneer at those models from a safe distance, we have to admit how much of our own silence is not high principle but plain fear, and how often, when we have spoken, we have done one of those very things. The verdict leaves weight. The problem with evangelism is not that we are too cowardly to be salesmen. It is that we were never meant to be salesmen at all, and we have been ashamed of the wrong thing.

keyScripture.why: Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, yet do it with gentleness and respect. The verse assumes the world asking us rather than us cornering the world, and it binds the answer to gentleness, naming both the readiness we lack and the manner the bad models abandon.

discussion.q: Be honest before we say anything spiritual. When the word evangelism comes up, what is your actual gut reaction, and what do you think is underneath it?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the real feeling before the correct one. For most people the honest reaction is dread, avoidance, or guilt, and naming it without judgment is the start. The aim is not to fix it tonight but to get it into the room, because the whole study depends on people admitting the fear they have been hiding in church. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Bell says some of our dread is shame and some of it is wisdom. Which of your fears about evangelism do you think are just cowardice, and which might be a true instinct that something was wrong with how you saw it done?
discussion.behind: Help the room sort the two kinds of fear. The point is not to excuse avoidance but to honor the part of the recoil that is right, the instinct against treating people as targets. If everyone concludes their fear is pure cowardice, they will only feel more ashamed. Let them find the wisdom buried in the dread.

discussion.q: Name the bad version you have seen. The salesman, the tract-pusher, the argument-winner, or another. What did it do to the person on the receiving end, and to your own willingness to ever try?
discussion.behind: Get specific about the caricatures. Most carry a memory of evangelism done badly, often done to them. The aim is to see clearly what is actually wrong with these models, that they reduce a person to a target, so the refusal is concrete and not abstract, and to feel why those models poisoned the well.

discussion.q: Bell admits that much of his own silence has been plain fear dressed up as principle, and that when he has spoken he has sometimes been the salesman or the arguer himself. Where have you done the same, either gone silent out of fear or spoken in a way you would not want done to you?
discussion.behind: Move to self-implication, gently. The temptation in this session is to feel superior to the bad evangelists. The aim is to bring everyone, the leader first, inside the indictment, to admit both the cowardly silence and the times we did the very thing we now criticize. Go first and name your own.

discussion.q: If the problem is not that we are too cowardly to be salesmen, but that we were never meant to be salesmen at all, what have you been ashamed of that you maybe should not have been, and what should you be ashamed of instead?
discussion.behind: Land the reframe. The relief is real, that the dread of being a pushy salesman is not a sign of weak faith but a healthy instinct. But do not let it become a free pass for silence. Help the room feel both halves, the wrong shame lifted and a truer responsibility named, so the session ends honest, not merely comforted.

objections.objection: I dread evangelism because I have seen what it does to people, the cornering, the pressure, the friendship that turns out to have been a recruitment effort the whole time. If avoiding that makes me a bad Christian, then fine, I am a bad Christian, but I will not do that to anyone.
objections.response: Bell does not want you to do that to anyone either, and neither does the New Testament, so hear the distinction with care, because it changes everything. The thing you are refusing is not evangelism. It is a counterfeit of it. The friendship that was really a recruitment effort, the conversation that was really a closing, the person reduced to a target, all of that deserves the recoil you feel, and your instinct against it is not weak faith but a true reading of something that was genuinely wrong. The gospel is not a product and a person is not a sale. But here is the gentle catch. The counterfeit is not the only option, and refusing the counterfeit is not the same as having nothing to give. There is a way of speaking of Jesus that is the opposite of the salesman, a witness who simply tells the truth about what they have seen and leaves the verdict to God and the person. You have not been refusing that. You have only ever seen the counterfeit, and you were right to refuse it. This study is about the other thing.

objections.objection: If I really loved Jesus the way I am supposed to, I would not be afraid to talk about him. The fear itself proves my faith is thin. So this whole study is just going to make me feel worse about a failure I already know I have.
objections.response: Stop there, because the premise is wrong and it has been quietly crushing you. Fear of evangelism is not proof of thin faith. It is, very often, the fear of being false, the fear of doing to someone what was done to you, the fear of cheapening something you actually treasure by selling it badly. That is not a small love. It can be a large one, frightened of mishandling what it loves. Bell carries this fear and came to Christ from atheism, so he knows both the dread of speaking and the experience of being spoken to badly. The apostle Paul told the Corinthians he came to them in weakness and fear and much trembling, and he was the boldest witness the church has known. The trembling did not disqualify him. So no, this study is not built to deepen your shame. It is built to lift the wrong shame off you and to show you that the thing you are afraid of being, the pushy salesman, is a thing you were never asked to be.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the real reason you have stayed silent about Jesus with the people closest to you, and is it cowardice, or is it a fear of doing to them something that was once done to you?
sessions.practice: This week, do not try to evangelize anyone. Instead, take an honest inventory. Write down, just for yourself, the people in your life who do not know Christ, and next to each name write the truest reason you have never spoken to them about him. Do not judge what you write. Then sort those reasons into two columns, the fears that are wisdom, a real instinct against treating them as a target, and the fears that are just fear. Sit with both columns and ask God to lift the false shame and to give you a witness that is the opposite of everything you have been right to dread.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have carried this dread in silence for years, sure that admitting it would expose how little we love you, and tonight we have finally said it out loud. Forgive us where our silence has been plain cowardice dressed up as principle. But thank you that some of our fear was wisdom, a true recoil from the salesman and the cornering and the friendship that was really a closing, things you never asked of us either. Lift off the shame we were never meant to carry. We do not want to be salesmen for you. Teach us to be witnesses. Show us the difference, and make us the kind of people whose word about you could be trusted because we treated the hearer as a person and not a target. Amen.
reflection: What is my honest gut reaction to evangelism, and how much of it is shame at a failure versus a healthy recoil from the counterfeit I have seen?
Where have I been the salesman, the tract-pusher, or the argument-winner myself, and what did it cost the person on the other end?
If I was never meant to be a salesman for Jesus, what false shame have I been carrying, and what truer responsibility have I been hiding behind it?
sessions.teaching: Let us start by saying the thing almost no one says in church. Most of us dread evangelism. We do not dread it a little. We dread it the way you dread a dental appointment you keep rescheduling, the way you dread the conversation you know you are supposed to have and keep finding reasons not to. And we carry that dread in silence, because in the church it feels unspeakable. To admit you would rather do almost anything than bring up Jesus at the dinner table feels like admitting you do not really love him, that your faith is a thin and embarrassed thing, and so we say nothing, and the dread hardens quietly into a settled avoidance, and we make our peace with being the kind of Christian who simply does not do that. So the first question of this entire study is not how. It is why. Why does this particular act, of all the things our faith asks of us, fill so many sincere believers with such reliable dread. And I am not asking it from the outside, as a man who has it figured out, because I do not. I came to faith from atheism, which means for most of my life I was on the other end of this, I was the project, the target, the soul somebody was trying to close, and I will tell you about that in a moment because it matters. But I also know the dread from inside the church, because I have it too. I have frozen at tables. I have let conversations sail right past the moment I should have spoken. I have rehearsed something to say to a neighbor and then said nothing for years. So when I ask why we dread it, I am asking about myself first. Now here is the thing I have come to believe, and it is the hinge of this whole opening session. Some of our dread is shame, and some of our dread is wisdom, and we have to learn to tell them apart, because we have been treating all of it as one failure. Part of the dread really is fear, plain and unspiritual, the fear of awkwardness, of rejection, of being thought a fool, of damaging a relationship we value. That part is worth naming honestly and bringing to God, and I will not pretend it away. But there is another part of the dread that is not weakness at all. It is a true instinct recoiling from something it has seen done badly. Because nearly all of us have watched evangelism done as a thing that should never be done to a human being, and the part of us that pulls back from that is not faithless. It is reading the situation correctly. So let me name the bad models plainly, the caricatures that poisoned the well, because until we name them we will keep thinking the dread is all about us, when half of it is about them. The first is the salesman. The salesman is closing a deal. The conversation is a sales process with a target outcome, the prayer prayed, the box checked, the convert notched, and the person across the table can feel it, can feel that they are not being met but worked, that there is a close coming and the warmth is a means to it. I know this one from the inside, because I was sold to. People who I later realized had befriended me as a strategy, whose interest evaporated the moment it was clear I was not going to pray their prayer on their timeline. I was a target, and I knew it, and it did not make me want their Jesus. It made me trust them less. The second is the tract-pusher. The tract-pusher has confused handing over a leaflet with handing over themselves. There is a place for good writing, I write for a living, but the tract-pusher uses the paper as a substitute for the relationship, a way to discharge the duty without the cost of actually being known by the person, and it can become a way of obeying the letter of evangelism while avoiding its entire heart, which was never a transaction of information but the offering of a life. The third is the argument-winner. This one tempts the smart and the well-read most, and it has tempted me. The argument-winner treats the unbeliever as a position to be defeated, a set of objections to be dismantled, and the goal, however it dresses itself up, is to win. And you can win. You can be right about every point and watch the person across from you close like a door, because no one was ever argued into the kingdom by someone who made them feel like a fool in front of their friends. The argument-winner wins the point and loses the person, and counts it a victory. Now here is where I have to stop pointing at these models from a safe distance, because the whole danger of a session like this is that we get to feel superior to the bad evangelists, to locate the problem entirely in those people over there, the pushy ones, the embarrassing ones, and to walk out clean. I cannot let us do that, because I cannot do it myself. When I have actually spoken about Jesus, and it has been rarer than it should be, I have been the salesman more than once, steering toward a close. I have hidden behind the equivalent of the tract, the shared article, the invitation to a service, anything to discharge the duty without the exposure of being known. And I have been the argument-winner, oh, I have been that, more interested in the rightness of my point than in the person I was supposedly loving. So the indictment lands on me before it lands on anyone in this room. Much of my own silence has been plain fear wearing the costume of principle, and much of my own speaking has been the very thing I now criticize. And so here is the verdict this first session leaves us with, and it is not the verdict we expected. We came in assuming the problem was that we are too cowardly, too embarrassed, too unwilling to push the way a bold Christian should push. That is not the problem. The problem is that we have been measuring ourselves against the salesman and feeling ashamed for not being a better one, when we were never meant to be a salesman at all. We have been ashamed of the wrong thing. The dread you feel at the thought of cornering someone, of treating a friend as a target, of trading your relationship for a closing, that dread is not your weakness. It is your conscience, and it is right. What you should be ashamed of is something quieter and truer, the silence that is just fear, the love that never found a voice, the good news you actually believe and have never once offered to anyone, not because you refused to be a salesman but because you never learned there was anything else to be. There is something else to be. It is older than the sales pitch and quieter than the argument and far harder to dread once you see it clearly. It is a witness. And that is where we are going next.

scriptureStudy.note: Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, yet do it with gentleness and respect. Notice the world asks first, and the answer is bound to gentleness, the opposite of the cornering salesman.

I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling. Paul, the boldest witness the church has known, names his own fear, which means the trembling we feel is not proof of disqualification but stands in the best of company.

Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt. The manner is named as gracious and wise, a posture toward outsiders, not a pitch aimed at targets.

We were ready to share with you not only the gospel of God but also our own selves, because you had become very dear to us. The opposite of the tract-pusher, the self is given along with the message, the person genuinely loved.

The Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, correcting opponents with gentleness. The argument-winner is named and refused, the goal is not to defeat the opponent but to win the person with gentleness.

When he saw the crowds, he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless. Jesus sees the lost as harassed and helpless, objects of compassion, not as targets to be closed, the posture under all true witness.

A woman of Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, give me a drink. Jesus opens not with a pitch but with a request, putting himself in her debt, beginning a real conversation with a real person rather than a sales approach.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the history of how evangelism came to feel like sales, because the salesman model is not the timeless shape of Christian witness but a fairly recent and culturally specific one, and seeing where it came from loosens its grip. The methods many of us absorbed, the planned presentation with its diagnostic questions and its closing prayer, were shaped in part by the revivalism of the nineteenth century, where the evangelist Charles Finney famously argued that revival was not a miracle but the predictable result of the right use of means, an outcome you could engineer with the right techniques. Set that beside the older picture, where the spread of the faith in its first three centuries happened largely through ordinary believers living visibly different lives within their neighborhoods and households, drawing questions rather than launching campaigns, and ask what was gained and what was lost when witness became a method with a target outcome. A serious group should weigh the way modern consumer culture trained us to see every interaction as a potential transaction, so that even our love became instrumental, a means to a conversion, and consider how deeply this distorts a gospel that is precisely not a product. Weigh, too, the genuine truth the revivalists were reaching for, that we ought to expect God to work and ought to actually invite people to follow Christ rather than hiding behind a vague niceness. The discipline is to keep the urgency and the invitation while refusing the salesmanship, to recover a witness that expects God to save without ever reducing a soul to a sale, and to grieve honestly how much of the church's evangelism has been the very thing the watching world rightly distrusts.

sessions.title: Witness, Not Salesman
sessions.aim: To recover the actual word the New Testament uses, witness, and to see how completely it differs from the salesman, a witness does not close a deal or manufacture an outcome but simply tells the truth about what they have seen, and to steelman the skeptic's honest distrust of being treated as a target.
sessions.summary: The Bible does not call us salesmen or closers or even, mostly, persuaders. It calls us witnesses, and the word is not decoration, it is the whole job description, and it changes everything once you take it seriously. A witness in a courtroom has one task, to tell the truth about what they have seen and heard, and a witness who tries to manufacture the verdict, who pressures the jury or fabricates certainty, is not a better witness but a corrupted one. The first question is what it does to our dread when we realize we were never assigned the verdict at all. Bell takes the strong form of the skeptic's distrust, and he takes it from the inside, because he was the skeptic. The honest unbeliever has often been treated as a target before, has felt the warmth that was really a tactic, and has every reason to distrust the Christian who approaches with an agenda. That distrust is not stubbornness. It is a reasonable response to having been handled. The session sits with the man born blind in John 9, dragged before the authorities and pressed to denounce the one who healed him, who refuses both to overclaim and to be silenced, and simply says what he knows, one thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. He does not have the theology worked out. He cannot answer every question. He testifies to the one thing he is sure of, the change in himself, and that testimony is unanswerable precisely because it claims no more than it knows. The turn is liberating. You are not responsible for closing the deal, manufacturing the outcome, or having every answer. You are responsible only for telling the truth about what you have actually seen, and leaving the verdict where it always belonged, with God and with the free person in front of you.

keyScripture.why: He answered, whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. The model witness claims only what he knows, refuses to overclaim or be silenced, and testifies to the one thing he is sure of, the change in himself, which is exactly what a witness is for and a salesman never does.

discussion.q: The Bible calls us witnesses, not salesmen or closers. What changes for you when you hear that the job is to tell the truth about what you have seen, not to manufacture the outcome?
discussion.behind: Open on the reframe at the center of the session. Most carry an unspoken assumption that evangelism means getting a result, and the dread is partly the dread of failing to produce it. The aim is to feel the relief and the responsibility of the word witness, that the verdict was never ours, only the testimony.

discussion.q: A witness in court who tries to force the verdict is a corrupted witness. Where have you seen Christians, or yourself, try to manufacture an outcome rather than just tell the truth, and what did it do to the credibility of the testimony?
discussion.behind: Press on the difference between testifying and manufacturing. The point is that pressure and overclaiming actually weaken the witness, they do not strengthen it. Help the room see that the salesman is not a more committed witness but a less trustworthy one, which reframes restraint as integrity rather than cowardice.

discussion.q: Bell says the skeptic's distrust of being treated as a target is not stubbornness but a reasonable response to having been handled. If you have ever been on the receiving end of an agenda dressed up as friendship, how did it feel, and what did it teach you about how not to treat people?
discussion.behind: Build empathy for the skeptic by accessing the room's own experience of being handled, whether by a salesman, a recruiter, or a Christian with an agenda. The aim is to honor the skeptic's distrust as reasonable, so the group stops seeing resistance as the problem to overcome and starts seeing trust as the thing to earn.

discussion.q: The man born blind says, one thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. He does not have the theology figured out and cannot answer every question. How does it free you to know that a witness only has to testify to what they actually know?
discussion.behind: Land the liberation of John 9. Many stay silent because they fear the questions they cannot answer. The aim is to free them from the impossible standard of the expert apologist and return them to the manageable, powerful task of the witness, saying truthfully what they have seen, which no one can refute.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has tried to be the closer, to manufacture a verdict that was never his to produce, and to overclaim a certainty he did not have. Where do you reach for outcomes that are not yours, or claim more than you actually know, and what would it look like to testify only to what you are sure of?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. The temptation is to overclaim, to feel we must defend more than we know or secure a result we cannot. Go first and name where you have done this. The aim is honest recognition that taking on the verdict is both exhausting and corrupting, and that the witness's restraint is freedom, not failure.

objections.objection: I can always tell when a Christian is being nice to me because they want to convert me. The friendliness has an agenda, and the moment I make clear I am not interested, the interest in me dries up. Why should I trust people who only seem to value me as a potential convert?
objections.response: You should not trust that, and Bell will be the first to say so, because he was you, the skeptic who could feel the agenda under the warmth and watched the interest evaporate the moment the close failed. Your distrust is not stubbornness or a hard heart. It is an accurate reading of having been handled, and the people who handled you that way were doing something genuinely wrong, treating you as a target rather than a person, which is the opposite of what they were sent to do. So hear this carefully, because it is the whole point. The friendship that was really a tactic was a counterfeit, and you were right to distrust it. But there is a real thing the counterfeit was imitating, a love that wants you to know Jesus precisely because it actually loves you, that would keep loving you whether or not you ever believe, that is not running a process on you. You have a right to test whether a Christian's care for you survives your saying no. The ones whose care does survive it are the witnesses. The ones whose care evaporates were the salesmen all along. Trust is earned, and you are allowed to make us earn it.

objections.objection: If I am supposed to be a witness, I have to be able to answer the hard questions, about suffering, about science, about other religions, and I cannot. I freeze. So I am not qualified to say anything, because the first real question will expose how little I actually know.
objections.response: Look at the man born blind, because he answers this objection for you across two thousand years. They pressed him with theological questions he could not answer, demanded he weigh in on whether the man who healed him was a sinner, tried to trap him in a debate he was not equipped for, and he refused the whole frame. He said, whether he is a sinner I do not know. One thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. He testified only to what he actually knew, the change in himself, and it was unanswerable precisely because he claimed nothing he could not stand behind. You are not the expert witness, the one who explains the mechanism. You are the eyewitness, the one who says what happened to you. When a question comes that you cannot answer, the honest words I do not know are not a failure of witness, they are part of it, and they are far more credible than a confident answer you do not actually have. You can say I do not know, and I can find out, or even I do not know, but here is the one thing I do know. The witness who admits the limit of his knowledge is more trustworthy, not less.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the one thing you actually know, the change in yourself you could testify to honestly, even if you could not answer a single hard question about it?
sessions.practice: This week, practice the discipline of the witness in ordinary conversation, with anyone, about anything. When you would normally reach to win an argument, to have the last word, to secure an outcome, stop and instead simply tell the truth about your own experience and leave the verdict to the other person. Notice how it feels to testify rather than to close. Then, set aside ten minutes and write down, in plain words, the one thing you know about what Christ has done in you, the change you could honestly testify to, claiming nothing you cannot stand behind. Do not polish it. Just get it true. Carry it with you, not as a script to deploy, but as the testimony you are ready to give if someone asks.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have been trying to do a job you never gave us, to manufacture verdicts that belong to you, to close deals on souls that were never ours to close, and it has exhausted us and corrupted our witness and made us into something the watching world rightly distrusts. Forgive us. Thank you that you have only ever asked us to be witnesses, to tell the truth about what we have seen, and that the verdict was always yours and the freedom always theirs. Teach us the restraint of the man born blind, to claim only what we know and to say I do not know without shame. Make our care for people survive their saying no, so that the skeptics among our friends can finally trust that we love them and not just the prayer we hoped they would pray. One thing we know. Let us learn to say it. Amen.
reflection: Where have I been trying to manufacture the verdict, to produce an outcome that was never mine, and how has taking on that impossible job kept me silent or made me false?
If I am honest, has my care for the people who do not believe survived their saying no, or did it evaporate the way the salesman's does, and what does that reveal?
What is the one thing I actually know, the change in myself I could testify to, and why have I let the questions I cannot answer keep me from saying the thing I can?
sessions.teaching: When Jesus tells his followers what they are going to be after he is gone, he does not reach for the language of sales or recruitment or persuasion. He reaches for a courtroom word. You will be my witnesses, he says, in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth. Witnesses. And we read past it because it has gone soft on us through overuse, but it is not a soft word, it is a precise one, and the whole shape of what we are supposed to be doing is hidden inside it, waiting to lift an enormous and false burden off our shoulders. So let us take the word seriously. What does a witness actually do. A witness in a courtroom has exactly one job, and it is a narrow one. They tell the truth about what they have seen and heard. That is all. A witness is not the lawyer, who builds the case and argues for the verdict. A witness is not the judge, who weighs and decides. A witness is not the jury, who renders the verdict. A witness has no power over the outcome and no responsibility for it. The witness's entire task is to say, truthfully and clearly, what they personally saw and heard, and then to step down. And here is the thing that should stop us. A witness who tries to do the other jobs is not a better witness. They are a corrupted one. A witness who pressures the jury, who manufactures a certainty they do not have, who shades the truth to push toward the verdict they want, who claims to have seen what they did not see, that witness has not served the truth more zealously. They have betrayed it. The overreaching witness is the discredited witness. Now hold that next to everything we said last session about the salesman, and feel what happens. The salesman's entire identity is bound up in the outcome, the close, the verdict. The salesman who does not close has failed. But the witness was never assigned the verdict at all. The verdict belongs to the judge and the jury, which is to say, in the matter of someone's soul, it belongs to God and to the free person themselves. We were never given that. We were given the testimony, and only the testimony, and the moment we try to seize the verdict, to manufacture the outcome, to close the deal, we stop being witnesses and become the corrupted thing. So the dread we carry, so much of it, is the dread of a job we were never given. We are exhausted and afraid because we have been trying to be the closer, and we keep failing, because closing was never ours to do. Lay it down. You are not responsible for the verdict. You are responsible for the truth about what you have seen. Now let me turn to the skeptic, because this is the session where we have to take the skeptic's distrust at full strength, and I take it from the inside, because I was the skeptic. The honest unbeliever has very often been treated as a target. They have felt the Christian warmth that turned out to be a tactic, the interest in them that evaporated the moment it was clear they were not going to convert on schedule, the friendship that was, all along, a recruitment effort with a smile on it. And when such a person becomes wary, when they can smell the agenda under the kindness and pull back, we are tempted to read that as a hard heart, as stubbornness, as the resistance of the spiritually closed. It is usually nothing of the kind. It is a reasonable response to having been handled. If someone had repeatedly been nice to you only as a means to an end, you would learn to distrust the niceness too. The skeptic's wariness is not the problem to be overcome. It is, very often, an accurate reading of how the church has actually treated people like them, and the honest thing is to grant it, to say, you are right to distrust the version of this you have seen, because it was not love, it was a transaction. Trust is not something the skeptic owes us. It is something we have to earn, and we earn it the way you earn any trust, by being the kind of person whose care does not depend on getting what you want. Now look at the witness I want to hold up for the whole rest of this study, because he is the pattern, and he is gloriously unqualified by our standards. In John chapter nine, Jesus heals a man who had been blind from birth, and immediately the man is dragged before the religious authorities, who are furious, because the healing happened on the Sabbath and threatens their whole framework. And they interrogate him. They press him to denounce the one who healed him. They demand he take a theological position on whether this Jesus is a sinner. They are educated, powerful, and hostile, and the man before them is a former beggar with no training, no credentials, no worked-out theology. And watch what he does, because it is a masterclass in witness. He does not pretend to know more than he knows. When they demand he pronounce on whether Jesus is a sinner, he refuses to overclaim. Whether he is a sinner I do not know, he says. He will not be pushed into testifying beyond his actual knowledge. But he also will not be silenced or talked out of the one thing he is certain of, the thing that happened to him, in his own body, that he cannot deny without lying. One thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. And there it is. The most powerful sentence in the chapter, and it is not an argument, not a doctrine, not a defense, not a close. It is a witness statement. He testifies to the one thing he knows, the change in himself, and he claims nothing beyond it, and that is exactly why it is unanswerable. They cannot refute it. They can intimidate him, and they do, they eventually throw him out, but they cannot touch his testimony, because he claimed only what he could stand behind, the evidence of his own healed eyes. He did not have the theology figured out. He could not have survived a debate. And he did not need to, because he was not the lawyer, he was the witness, and the witness only has to be true. Feel how this lifts the burden. You do not have to answer every question. You do not have to win the argument about suffering or science or the other religions. When the hard question comes, the most powerful thing you can say is often I do not know, and it is not a failure of witness, it is part of one, because the witness who admits the edge of his knowledge is the witness you can trust about the center of it. You are not the expert witness who explains the mechanism. You are the eyewitness who says what happened to you. And I have to put myself inside the indictment here, because I have not been the man born blind. I have been the man who tried to be the closer, who reached for verdicts that were never mine, who felt the conversation slipping and squeezed harder, who claimed more certainty than I actually had because I thought confidence was the same as faithfulness. I have overclaimed. I have manufactured. I have treated the restraint of the honest witness as if it were a weakness to be overcome rather than the very integrity that makes a witness believable. So this is the verdict the session leaves, and it is a freeing one if you will let it land. You were never the salesman, and you were never the judge. You are a witness. Your job is to tell the truth about what you have seen, all of it and none beyond it, and then to step down and leave the verdict where it has belonged from the beginning, with a God who is far better at saving people than you are, and with a free human being whose yes, if it ever comes, has to be their own. One thing I know. That is enough. It was enough to defeat the experts in John nine, and it is enough for you.

scriptureStudy.note: One thing I know, that though I was blind, now I see. The model witness claims only what he knows, the change in himself, refusing both to overclaim and to be silenced, and it is unanswerable precisely because it claims no more than it knows.

You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. Jesus names the role with a courtroom word, witness, not salesman or closer, defining the job as testimony to what has been seen.

The man reasons from the one thing he knows, never has it been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. His simple testimony to his own healing, not a worked-out theology, is what silences the experts.

We cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard. Peter and John define their witness as testimony to experience, what they have seen and heard, the eyewitness posture rather than the argument or the sales pitch.

You will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. Paul's commission is framed as witness to his own experience, even Paul the scholar is sent first as an eyewitness to what happened to him.
Come and see. Philip does not argue Nathanael out of his skepticism but invites him to look, the witness pointing to the evidence rather than manufacturing the verdict for the skeptic.

That which we have seen and heard we proclaim also to you. John grounds the whole proclamation in eyewitness testimony, what was seen and heard and touched, the witness reporting rather than the salesman closing.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up what the courtroom metaphor actually carries, because witness is not a casual term the New Testament reaches for by accident but a settled image with weight, and the Greek word behind it, martys, is the root of our word martyr, which tells you something the salesman model never could. A witness, in the biblical sense, is someone who testifies to the truth regardless of the cost, and at the extreme the cost is everything, which is how the word for witness became the word for the one who dies rather than deny what they have seen. The salesman walks away when the close fails. The witness stays with the truth even when it costs them, because their job was never to produce a result but to be faithful to what is real. Set this beside the modern reduction of evangelism to communication strategy, the right script, the right approach, the measurable outcome, and ask what is lost when testimony becomes technique, when a word that once meant willingness to die for the truth becomes a method for managing a conversation. A serious group should weigh the epistemology of testimony itself, the way that so much of what any of us knows, in history, in science, in our own families, we know not by direct proof but by trusting reliable witnesses, which means testimony is not a weak form of knowledge but one of the basic ways human beings come to know anything at all. The honest skeptic who demands proof rather than testimony has often not noticed how much of their own confident knowledge rests on trusting witnesses they never independently verified. The discipline is to recover the dignity and the limits of the witness, to testify faithfully to what we have actually seen, to refuse both the overclaiming that corrupts testimony and the silence that withholds it, and to let the truth, and the God of truth, carry the weight of the verdict.

sessions.title: Presence Before Words
sessions.aim: To see that witness is carried first by a life and a community before it is ever carried by a sentence, that the congregation living a visibly different life together is what makes the question askable, and to recover hospitality as witness rather than as a tactic.
sessions.summary: We have been assuming evangelism is mainly a matter of words, of finding the right thing to say, which is part of why we dread it, because we feel verbally unequipped. But the New Testament puts a life before the words, and a shared life before an individual one. The first question is what makes anyone ask us about our hope in the first place, because the verse we keep quoting assumes they ask. Bell takes up the claim that the congregation, the actual community of believers living a visibly different life together, is what makes the gospel believable, the lived demonstration that the words point to. The argument is that the gospel cannot be finally understood as a set of ideas argued in the abstract, but is made askable by a community whose common life is itself the evidence, the people among whom the claims of the gospel are seen to be true before they are heard to be explained. The session steelmans the skeptic who says he has heard the words a thousand times and seen nothing in the lives to make them credible, and grants that the words have very often been contradicted by the lives, that the church has frequently been the strongest argument against its own message. Then it recovers hospitality, the open table and the open home, not as a softening-up tactic before the real evangelism of words, but as itself a primary form of witness, the place where a person is welcomed and known before they are ever asked to decide anything. The turn leaves weight. The question that lets us speak is usually one we did not engineer with a clever opener, but one that a watching person finally asks because something in the way we live together made them wonder, and most of us have not lived in a way that makes anyone wonder anything.

keyScripture.why: By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. Jesus locates the persuasive evidence not in the rightness of the argument but in the love among the disciples, the shared life that the watching world reads as the proof, making the community itself the witness before any word is spoken.

discussion.q: The verse we quote, be ready to give a reason for your hope, assumes someone asks. What is it about a life or a community that makes a watching person actually ask, and has anyone ever asked you?
discussion.behind: Open on the overlooked assumption. We obsess over the answer and ignore the question, and the question only comes when a life provokes it. The aim is to move the room from what do I say to what kind of life makes anyone curious, and to notice honestly whether their lives have provoked any questions at all.

discussion.q: The claim is that the community of believers living a visibly different life together is what makes the gospel believable. When, if ever, has a group of Christians living a certain way made faith credible to you or to someone you know, more than any argument did?
discussion.behind: Get at the communal nature of witness. We default to thinking of evangelism as an individual verbal act. The aim is to feel that a shared life is the primary witness, that people are persuaded by seeing something real among a people more than by hearing a case made by an individual.

discussion.q: Bell grants that the church has often been the strongest argument against its own message, that the words have been contradicted by the lives. Where have you seen that contradiction, and how does it raise the stakes on the life we actually live together?
discussion.behind: Honor the skeptic's hardest charge, that the lives have not matched the words. The aim is not to wallow but to feel the weight, that a community whose life contradicts its message has already lost the witness, and that this is on us, not on the skeptic's hard heart.

discussion.q: Hospitality, the open table and the open home, is offered here as witness itself, not as a tactic before the real evangelism. What is the difference between welcoming someone because you love them and welcoming them as a step in a conversion process, and can people tell?
discussion.behind: Press on the integrity of hospitality. The temptation is to instrumentalize welcome, to make the meal a means to the close. The aim is to recover hospitality as an end in itself, a real form of love and witness, and to feel that people can sense the difference between being welcomed and being worked.

discussion.q: Bell admits his own life and his own household have often not been the kind that makes anyone wonder anything. Where does your life, or our life together as a church, fail to provoke a single question, and what would have to change?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication, communal and personal. The aim is honest recognition that the problem is often not that we lack the right words but that we live in a way that prompts no questions at all. Go first. Name where your own life is unremarkable to the watching world, and let the room own it together.

objections.objection: I have heard the Christian message a thousand times. I do not need more words. What I have never seen is a group of Christians whose actual lives made me think there was anything to it. The lives contradict the words, so why would more words help?
objections.response: They would not, and Bell grants the whole of this, because it is the hardest and most honest charge the skeptic makes, and the church has earned it. You are right that more words are not the answer when the words have already been contradicted by the lives, and you are right that a community whose common life looks no different from the world around it has already undercut everything it might say. The New Testament agrees with you, which is why Jesus said the world would know his disciples not by their arguments but by their love for one another, staking the credibility of the whole thing on a visible, shared life. So the failure you have seen is real, and it is the church's failure, not your hardness. But notice what your own objection assumes, that there could be a community whose life actually made the words believable, that you would know it if you saw it, that the problem is precisely the absence of the thing, not the impossibility of it. That is exactly the claim, that the gospel is made askable by a people whose life together is its evidence. You have not seen it, and that is an indictment of us. The honest response is not more words but a different common life, and you have every right to keep withholding belief until you see one.

objections.objection: If hospitality is really just a strategy to get people in the door so you can convert them, then it is the same manipulation as everything else, just warmer. The free meal is the bait. Why is that any better than the salesman?
objections.response: It is not any better, and if that is what it is, you should refuse it, because hospitality used as bait is the salesman's tactic with a tablecloth, and people can feel the agenda under the welcome the same way they feel it under the friendliness. So the distinction is everything, and it is a real one. True hospitality is not a means to an end, it is an end, the actual love of an actual person, welcomed and fed and known whether or not they ever believe, with no close coming, no agenda underneath, no withdrawal of warmth if they decline. The test is simple and the guest applies it without being told. Does the welcome survive a no. If you come to the table and make clear you have no interest in the host's faith, and the welcome continues unchanged, you were genuinely welcomed. If the warmth cools, you were being worked. The early church turned the ancient world upside down partly by welcoming the unwelcome, the poor, the sick, the stranger, with a love that asked nothing in return, and the watching world found it bewildering and magnetic precisely because it was not a transaction. The meal is not the bait. The meal is the message, or part of it, and a host whose love is real has nothing to hide and nothing to close.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If a watching person spent a month observing how you and the Christians around you actually live, would anything they saw make them wonder, or would your life raise no question at all?
sessions.practice: This week, set a table. Invite someone into your home or to a meal, someone outside the faith if you can, and welcome them with no agenda whatsoever, no opener planned, no close intended, simply the genuine love of a guest. Do not steer the conversation toward Jesus. Just be the kind of host whose welcome would survive their saying no to anything. Notice what it does to you to love someone without an outcome in view. And as a community exercise, ask honestly, with the people you worship beside, whether your common life together would make any watching person curious, and name one concrete way your shared life could become more visibly different, more clearly marked by the love Jesus said the world would recognize.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have treated witness as a problem of words while living lives that raised no questions and a common life that looked no different from the world we were sent to. Forgive us. Too often we have been the strongest argument against the very message we claim, the words contradicted by the lives, and the skeptics who walked away saw clearly what we refused to see. Make us a people whose life together is itself the evidence, marked by the love you said the world would recognize. Teach us to set tables that welcome the stranger with no agenda underneath, to love people whether or not they ever believe, so that the welcome survives every no. Let our shared life become the kind of thing that makes a watching person finally wonder. And when they ask, may they find the words were true all along, because the lives were true first. Amen.
reflection: Does my life, and the common life of the Christians around me, actually provoke any questions, or does it look so much like the world that no one ever wonders?
Where has the church I am part of, or my own life, contradicted its message, becoming an argument against the gospel rather than for it?
What would it mean to practice hospitality as real love rather than as a tactic, to welcome people in a way that would survive their saying no to everything I believe?
sessions.teaching: We have been assuming, without quite saying it, that evangelism is mainly a problem of words, that if we just had the right thing to say, the right opener, the right answer to the hard question, we could do this. And so we dread it as the verbally unequipped dread public speaking, sure that the failure is in our tongues. But the New Testament keeps doing something that should reorient us. It keeps putting a life before the words, and a shared life before any individual one. Go back to the verse we have been leaning on, the one from Peter, be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in you. We quote it as a command to be verbally prepared, and it is partly that. But look at what it assumes, the thing we read right past. It assumes someone is asking. Be ready to give a reason to anyone who asks you. The whole sentence presupposes a watching person who has become curious enough to ask a question, and here is what should stop us cold. What makes anyone ask. People do not generally walk up to strangers and inquire about the source of their hope. The question comes when a life has provoked it, when someone has watched the way you handle a loss, or a betrayal, or a fear, or money, or your enemies, and seen something they cannot account for, something that does not fit, and the strangeness of it finally surfaces as a question. The reason most of us are never asked is not that we lack the right answer. It is that our lives have not raised the question. There is nothing to explain, because there is nothing visibly different to be explained. And the New Testament goes further than the individual life, because it locates the deepest witness in a shared one. On the night before he died, Jesus did not tell his disciples that the world would know them by the rigor of their arguments or the persuasiveness of their individual pitches. He said, by this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. The watching world's evidence is the love among the disciples, the quality of their common life, the way they treat each other. The community itself is the witness. And this is the claim I want to put at the center of this session, that the gospel is not finally understood as a set of abstract ideas argued in a vacuum, but is made believable, made askable, by a community whose common life is the demonstration that the words are true. The argument runs like this. The claims of the gospel, that there is forgiveness, that enemies can be reconciled, that the poor have dignity, that death does not have the last word, these are not the kind of claims that can be proven on a whiteboard. They are claims that have to be seen to be believed, seen at work in an actual people, and the place they are seen, or fail to be seen, is the congregation, the community of believers living visibly by them. The community is the lens through which the watching world reads whether the gospel is true. When the church genuinely forgives, genuinely welcomes the outsider, genuinely shares its goods, genuinely loves across the lines the world cannot cross, the gospel becomes legible, and people start to ask. When the church does none of those things, the gospel becomes illegible, no matter how many words are spoken, because the demonstration contradicts the claim. Now I have to grant the skeptic his hardest charge, and I have to grant all of it, because it is true. The skeptic says, I have heard the words a thousand times and I have never once seen the lives to match them. And he is right more often than we can bear to admit. The church has, with grim reliability, been the strongest argument against its own message. We have preached forgiveness and nursed grudges for decades. We have proclaimed the dignity of the poor and built our buildings to keep them comfortably out. We have announced reconciliation and split into a thousand tribes that will not eat together. We have said come as you are and meant come as we are. And the watching world has not failed to notice. The skeptic who walked away because the lives contradicted the words did not have a hard heart. He had working eyes. He read the demonstration, and the demonstration argued against the message, and he believed the demonstration, which is exactly what John 13 said he would do. So the stakes on the life we live together are not low and they are not optional. The common life of the church is not the soft preliminary to the real work of evangelism. It is the evangelism, or it is the counter-evangelism, and there is no neutral. Now let me recover one specific thing, because it is concrete and it is something every one of us can actually do, and that is hospitality. The open table and the open home run through the whole story of God's people. Israel was commanded to love the stranger, to leave the edges of the field unharvested for him, because they themselves had been strangers. Jesus ate with the people no one else would eat with, and it was scandalous, and it was a sermon. The early church was known for taking in the abandoned, feeding the hungry, welcoming the traveler, caring for the sick during the plagues when others fled, and this hospitality was not a softening-up tactic before the real evangelism of words. It was itself the witness, the visible, edible, unmistakable demonstration that something had changed in these people. And here we have to be careful, because we are so trained by the salesman model that we will immediately try to weaponize even this, to make the meal a means to the close, the welcome a step in a process. The moment we do that, we have ruined it, and the guest will feel it, because hospitality with an agenda is just the salesman with a casserole. True hospitality is not a means to an end. It is the love of an actual person, welcomed and fed and known whether or not they ever come to believe anything, and the test of whether it is real is whether the welcome survives a no. If a guest comes to your table and makes plain they have no interest in your faith, and your warmth toward them does not cool by a single degree, then you have welcomed them, and that welcome is itself a word about the God you serve, spoken in a language deeper than speech. If the warmth cools when the conversion does not look likely, you were never hosting them. You were processing them. And here is where I have to climb down off the platform and into the indictment, because this session indicts me as much as any, maybe more. My own life has too often not been the kind that makes anyone wonder anything. I have handled losses no differently than my unbelieving neighbors handled theirs. My household has not always been a place marked by a love so strange that a guest left puzzled by it. I have hoarded my home and my table out of busyness and self-protection, kept my hospitality for the people who were already family, and wondered, with a kind of dishonesty, why no one ever asks me about my hope. They do not ask because there is nothing to ask about. My life has raised no question, and you cannot answer a question no one has reason to pose. So this is the verdict, and it leaves weight, because it shifts the whole problem and there is no easy exit from it. We have been losing sleep over what to say, and the deeper issue was never what we would say but who we would be, alone and together. The question that finally lets us speak is almost never one we engineered with a clever opener. It is one a watching person asks because something in the way we live, and especially in the way we live together, made them wonder. Most of us have not lived in a way that makes anyone wonder anything, and most of our churches have not either, and that, not our verbal awkwardness, is the heart of why we are so rarely asked. The good news buried in the hard verdict is that this is something we can actually change, and it does not require eloquence. It requires a life. It requires a table. It requires a community whose love for one another is strange enough to be noticed. Build that, and the questions will come, and when they come, you will find you have less to dread than you thought, because by then the hardest part of the witness will already have been spoken, without a word, by the life.

scriptureStudy.note: By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. Jesus stakes the world's recognition of his people on the love among them, the shared life as the evidence rather than the argument.

Be ready to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you. The verse assumes a watching person asks, which means a life has first provoked the question rather than a pitch having launched it.

Day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, and the Lord added to their number. The growth follows a shared life of table and generosity, not a campaign.

Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father. The witness is visible works seen by watching others, the life as the lamp before any word is spoken.

Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality. Hospitality is commanded as a mark of the transformed life, the open hand and the open home as ordinary Christian practice, not as evangelistic tactic.

Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. Hospitality is aimed at the stranger, the outsider, the one not yet family, the welcome extended before any relationship is established.

When you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. Jesus commends the hospitality that expects no return, the welcome that survives because it was never a transaction.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the claim that the congregation is the hermeneutic of the gospel, which is the careful form of what this session has been arguing, and which Lesslie Newbigin set out in The Gospel in a Pluralist Society, published in 1989. Newbigin, a missionary bishop who spent decades in India and then returned to a Western culture he found had quietly stopped believing, asked how the gospel could be made credible to a society that no longer shared its assumptions, and his answer was that the only hermeneutic of the gospel, the only lens through which a watching world can interpret whether the good news is true, is a congregation of men and women who believe it and live by it. Not the argument, not the apologetic, not the campaign, but the community whose common life is the evidence. The idea presses against the deep modern assumption that truth is established by neutral reasoning available to any individual mind, and insists instead that the truth of the gospel is the kind of thing known through participation in a people who embody it, seen before it is proven. Set this beside the long history of the early church, where the visible care of Christians for the sick and the abandoned, documented even by hostile observers, did more to commend the faith than any treatise, and ask what has been lost in a church that has come to think of evangelism as a verbal and individual transaction rather than the overflow of a visibly distinct common life. A serious group should weigh the heavy responsibility this lays on the local church, that its ordinary life together, how it handles money and conflict and the outsider and the poor, is not the private business of the congregation but the public evidence on which the watching world weighs the gospel. The discipline is to take the common life with the seriousness the witness demands, to build a community whose love is legible enough to provoke the question, and to recover hospitality and shared life as the primary language in which the gospel is spoken, the word made visible before it is ever made audible.

sessions.title: Telling Your Story
sessions.aim: To recover personal testimony from the formulaic before-and-after that has cheapened it, to give the witness permission to tell the truth about their own faith including its doubt and its cost, and to see that the most credible testimony is the one honest enough to admit what it is still costing.
sessions.summary: Eventually the witness has words to speak, and the most natural and powerful of them is the testimony, the telling of one's own story. But testimony has been ruined for many by a formula, the polished before-and-after, the dramatic rescue from the depths to the heights, packaged with a neat resolution and an implied altar call, and the ordinary Christian whose story does not fit the template concludes they have no testimony worth telling. The first question is why we ever believed testimony had to be a tidy conversion narrative with a clean ending. Bell takes the strong form of the honest person's resistance, that the polished testimony feels false, that real faith is not a before-and-after but an ongoing thing with doubt still in it, and that a story scrubbed of its doubt and its cost is not more credible but less, because everyone knows real life does not work that way. He grants that the formula has produced a generation of testimonies no thoughtful person believes, precisely because they are too clean. The session recovers testimony as honest witness, the truthful telling of what you have actually seen and what it has actually cost, doubt included, struggle included, the parts that are still unresolved included. It argues that the most credible witness is not the one with the most dramatic rescue but the one most honest about the price, because admitting the cost is what proves the testimony is not a sales pitch. The turn leaves weight. The story worth telling is not the one where everything got fixed, but the true one, where you found something worth the cost and are still, some days, counting the cost, and that honesty, not the polish, is what a skeptic can finally trust.

keyScripture.why: Go home to your friends and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you. Jesus sends the healed man not with a doctrine to argue or a formula to recite but with his own story to tell among the people who know him, testimony as the truthful account of what God has done in a particular life.

discussion.q: Many of us have heard the polished before-and-after testimony, the dramatic rescue with the tidy ending. Why do you think we ever came to believe a testimony had to look like that, and what does it do to people whose story does not fit?
discussion.behind: Open by exposing the formula. Many conclude they have no testimony because theirs lacks the drama and the clean resolution. The aim is to name the template as a distortion, not the standard, and to free the ordinary believer whose story is real but undramatic to see it as a true testimony nonetheless.

discussion.q: Bell says a testimony scrubbed of its doubt and its cost is less credible, not more, because everyone knows real life does not work that way. Have you ever heard a testimony that felt too clean to believe, and what was missing from it?
discussion.behind: Press on the credibility of honesty. The point is counterintuitive, that the polish undermines rather than strengthens. Help the room feel that the doubt and the unresolved parts are not weaknesses to hide but the very things that make a story believable to a thoughtful hearer.

discussion.q: The most credible witness is often the one most honest about the cost. What has following Jesus actually cost you, and have you ever told that part of your story, or only the parts that sound like gain?
discussion.behind: Get at the cost, which the formula erases. We tend to tell the upside and hide the price. The aim is to recover the cost as part of the testimony, to feel that admitting what faith has cost is precisely what proves it is not a sales pitch, because no salesman advertises the price.

discussion.q: Real faith is often an ongoing thing with doubt still in it, not a finished before-and-after. How honest are you able to be about the doubt that is still in your own faith, and who have you ever been honest about it with?
discussion.behind: Make room for ongoing doubt as part of an honest testimony. Many hide their doubt, believing a real testimony has none. The aim is to free them to tell the truth, including the unresolved, and to feel that a faith honest about its doubt is more trustworthy than one that pretends to have none.

discussion.q: Bell admits he has told the cleaned-up version of his own story, the dramatic atheist-to-believer arc, while hiding the doubt that is still in it and the cost he is still counting. Where do you tell the polished version of your story and hide the true one, and why?
discussion.behind: Close with self-implication. The temptation is to perform a testimony rather than tell one. Go first and name where you have polished your own story and hidden its harder truths. The aim is honest recognition that the cleaned-up testimony is a kind of dishonesty, and that the true one is harder and better.

objections.objection: Every testimony I have ever heard sounds the same and sounds fake. I was lost, I was miserable, I found Jesus, now everything is wonderful. Nobody's life actually works like that. The neatness is exactly why I do not believe a word of it.
objections.response: You are right not to believe that, and Bell would not ask you to, because the neat before-and-after you are describing is often not a true testimony but a performance of one, and your instinct that real life does not resolve that cleanly is not cynicism, it is accuracy. A faith advertised as the end of all struggle is being sold, not witnessed to, and the polish that is supposed to make it attractive is exactly what makes it unbelievable to anyone paying attention. So hear the distinction. A true testimony is not the absence of struggle but the presence of something worth the struggle. The honest witness does not say everything is wonderful now. He says I found something I believe is true and good, and it has cost me, and some days I still doubt, and I am still counting the cost, and I would not go back. That story you might believe, precisely because it does not pretend. The healed man Jesus sent home was told to tell what the Lord had done for him, his actual story, not a formula, and the most credible Christians you will ever meet are the ones honest enough to tell you what it has cost them and what they still wrestle with. The neatness you distrust is a sign of a sales pitch. The honesty you have never been offered is the sign of a witness.

objections.objection: I cannot give a testimony because I still have doubts. My faith is not some settled, finished thing. If I am honest about how much I still wrestle, I will undermine the very thing I am supposed to be commending, so it is better to say nothing.
objections.response: It is the reverse, and believing otherwise has silenced a great many honest Christians who would have made the best witnesses in the room. Your doubt does not disqualify your testimony, it authenticates it. A faith presented as having no doubts in it is a faith no thoughtful person believes, because they know their own minds and know that honest belief in things unseen is held alongside real wrestling, not in the absence of it. When you say I believe this, and I still wrestle with that, and here is what holds me anyway, you are not undermining the gospel, you are telling the truth about it in a way that a doubter can finally trust, because you have just shown them that faith and doubt are not strangers, that one can hold the first while still feeling the second. Bell came to faith from atheism and will tell you plainly that the doubt did not vanish at conversion, that he has prayed into silence and wrestled with the hardest questions and believes still, not despite the honesty but through it. The father in Mark who cried out, I believe, help my unbelief, gave one of the truest testimonies in the Gospels, and it had the doubt right inside it. Tell that story. It is the one people can trust.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What is the true version of your story, the one with the doubt still in it and the cost you are still counting, and who have you never told it to because you only ever tell the polished one?
sessions.practice: This week, write your testimony twice. First, write the polished version, the clean before-and-after, the way you would say it if you were trying to make faith sound attractive. Then set it aside and write the true version, the one with the doubt still in it, the cost you are still paying, the parts that did not resolve, the thing you found that you believe is worth it anyway. Notice how different they are, and notice which one you would actually trust if someone told it to you. Then, this week, tell some part of the true version to one person, not as a pitch, not aiming at any outcome, simply as the honest account of what you have seen and what it has cost. Pay attention to how it lands when you tell the truth instead of the formula.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we have learned to tell the cleaned-up version of our stories, the dramatic rescue with the tidy ending, and in polishing them we made them into things no honest person could believe. Forgive us for trading the truth of what you have done for a formula that sounds impressive and rings false. We have hidden our doubt, sure it disqualified us, when it was the very thing that made our witness trustworthy. We have hidden the cost, advertising only the gain, until our testimony sounded like a sales pitch. Teach us to tell the true story instead, the one with the wrestling still in it and the price still being paid, the one where we found something worth the cost and are still, some days, counting it. Let our honesty be the thing the skeptic can finally trust. Tell them how much the Lord has done, you said. Help us tell it true. Amen.
reflection: Where have I believed I had no testimony worth telling because my story lacked the drama and the clean resolution of the formula?
What has following Jesus actually cost me, and why do I tell only the parts that sound like gain and hide the parts that sound like loss?
How honest am I willing to be about the doubt still in my own faith, and could telling the true, unresolved version of my story be more credible than the polished one?
sessions.teaching: Eventually the witness has to speak, and the most natural words a witness has, the words even the most reluctant among us can find, are the words of our own story. Not an argument, not a doctrine, not someone else's case, but the simple account of what we have seen and what has happened to us. When Jesus heals the man possessed in the country of the Gerasenes, the man begs to come with him, and Jesus says no, and gives him instead a commission so plain that any of us could carry it out. Go home to your friends, he says, and tell them how much the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you. Not, go construct an apologetic. Not, go win the argument. Go home and tell your story to the people who know you. That is testimony, and it is the most available form of witness there is, because no one knows your story better than you do, and no one can refute it, because it happened to you. And yet testimony has been ruined for a great many people, and we have to be honest about how. It has been ruined by a formula. Somewhere along the way we absorbed a template for what a testimony is supposed to be, and the template goes like this. There is a dramatic before, the depths, the addiction, the rock bottom, the wreckage. Then there is a moment, sharp and datable, the rescue, the conversion, the night everything changed. And then there is a glorious after, the restored life, the resolved struggle, the happy ending, with an implied invitation hanging off the end of it, an altar call dressed up as autobiography. And this template has done two pieces of damage at once, and they pull in opposite directions. To the ordinary believer whose story does not fit it, it whispers that they have no testimony at all. If you were not rescued from some spectacular pit, if you cannot point to a single datable night, if your coming to faith was slow and undramatic and is frankly still in progress, the template tells you to stay quiet, because your story is not impressive enough to be worth telling. And to the skeptic on the other end, the same template whispers something else, that the whole thing is fake. Because the skeptic has heard a hundred of these polished arcs, and he knows, from his own life, that real human stories do not resolve that cleanly, and the very neatness that was supposed to make the testimony attractive is exactly what makes it unbelievable. So let me take the honest person's resistance at full strength, because I share it. The polished testimony feels false, and it feels false because it is, at least partly. Real faith is not a before-and-after. It is an ongoing thing, with doubt still in it, with struggle still in it, with questions that did not get answered and wounds that did not get healed and a cost that is still being paid. A story scrubbed clean of all that is not a more powerful witness. It is a less credible one, because everyone who is paying attention knows that life does not work that way, and a testimony that pretends it does has just told the hearer that the witness is either lying or not paying attention to his own life. The formula has produced a whole generation of testimonies that no thoughtful person believes, and they do not believe them precisely because they are too clean. So we have to recover testimony as honest witness, and the recovery turns on two things the formula erased, the doubt and the cost. Take the doubt first.
